survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD Survey of Adult Skills country note reports descriptive results for France based on a household survey of adults aged 16–65 in 2022–23. The note states that the sample was drawn to be representative of about 39.8 million adults aged 16–65 residing in France and that analyses were conducted to ensure no significant bias from non-response, but it does not provide the specific weight variable names or replicate-weight methodology. The assessment proficiency scales are derived from performance on literacy, numeracy, and adaptive problem solving tasks administered on tablets, and proficiency is reported on 500-point scales with proficiency levels. For analysts using the underlying microdata, complex survey design weights are typically required to produce population-representative estimates; however, this country note does not document the exact weight variables (e.g., final student weights) or any replicate scheme, so the precise weighting implementation cannot be verified from the provided text.

Otherwise, the note does not specify additional analytic exclusions (e.g., missing background variables) for the reported descriptive results.

data.outcome_summary: The OECD Survey of Adult Skills 2023 country note for France summarizes adults’ proficiency in three domains—literacy, numeracy, and adaptive problem solving—assessed in 2022–23 among adults aged 16–65. France participated for the second time (first participation in 2011–12), enabling comparisons over time and with other participating countries/economies. The assessment was administered exclusively on digital tablets and proficiency is reported on 500-point scales, with discrete proficiency levels used to describe what adults can do at each level. In France, mean performance is below the OECD average in all three domains (literacy 255, numeracy 257, adaptive problem solving 248), and around 28–30% of adults score at or below Level 1 across the domains. The note also reports subgroup patterns (e.g., lower proficiency among older adults) and associations between higher numeracy and better employment and wage outcomes, as well as links between high proficiency and well-being/civic engagement, while excluding doorstep-only respondents from cross-cycle comparisons.
